paragraphs: When a regional grocery chain introduced a loyalty card, its managers expected sales per customer to rise, and in the first year they did: card holders spent roughly twelve percent more per visit than non-holders. The chain's executives took this as proof that the program worked. Yet card holders had signed up voluntarily, and the shoppers most inclined to enroll were precisely those who already shopped frequently and bought in volume. In other words, the difference in spending may have existed before the card did. Only by comparing holders' spending with their own spending in the year before enrolling could the chain say how much, if any, of the increase the card itself produced.
